C. Both baskets are specified to have the same 10% per annum linear growth trend and a stationary return distribution with constant long run volatility.

Write the price after removing the known deterministic drift as $\tilde P_t = P_t /1.10^{\,t}$. By construction $E[\tilde P_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=\tilde P_t$, i.e. the de-trended return is stationary with zero mean. In levels this is $E[P_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_t]=1.10^{\Delta}P_t$, the same drift-adjusted martingale for A and for B, A being the degenerate zero-variance case.

Linearity of expectation is preserved under any $\mathcal F_t$-measurable liquidation plan. Let $\Theta_s\ge0$ be the fraction of the position liquidated on $[30+s,30+s+ds]$ in the 31st year, $\int_0^1\Theta_s ds =1$. Then

$E\Big[\int_0^1 P_{30+s}\Theta_s ds\Big|\mathcal F_{30}\Big]
 =P_{30}E\Big[\int_0^1 1.10^{s}\Theta_s ds\Big|\mathcal F_{30}\Big]
 =P_{30}\int_0^1 1.10^{s}\Theta_s ds,$

so the unconditional mean is $E[P_{30}]\,E[\int_0^1 1.10^{s}\Theta_s ds]$. The best you can do in expectation with an adapted $\Theta$ is to postpone as much as possible, i.e. $\Theta_s=\delta_{s=1}$, giving $E[V]=P_0 1.10^{31}$.

The 31st year is a bounded stopping problem for a drift-adjusted martingale. Optional stopping therefore gives $E[P_{\tau}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=1.10^{\tau-30}P_{30}$ for any admissible $\tau\in[30,31]$. Volatility changes the dispersion of $P_{B,\tau}$ and the shape of the distribution, and indeed $E[\max_{30\le t\le31}P_{B,t}]>E[P_{B,31}]$ as a random variable, but $\max_t P_t$ is not an adapted payoff. The ex-ante expectation of any pre-committed, adapted liquidation rule, and in particular the expectation of the value attainable by an optimal adapted rule, remains the drift-implied mean $P_0 1.10^{31}$.

Hence after de-trending the two processes are martingales in returns, the first moment is pinned down by the 10% drift alone, and the unconditional expected liquidation value is the same for the deterministic basket A and the high-volatility drifted basket B. Volatility adds risk and reshapes the distribution, not the mean.

C. Since the return distribution is stationary and the 10% per year trend is known to both baskets, the drift-adjusted price is a martingale in returns for both A and B.

For A, P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s., so E[P^A_{t+Δ}|F_t]=1.10^Δ P^A_t.
For B, by construction E[P^B_{t+Δ}|F_t]=1.10^Δ P^B_t with zero-mean stationary innovations around the 10% trend. The weekly ±20% moves and the long-run constant autocovariance change only second moments, not the first.

E[ ∫_0^1 P_{30+s} θ_s ds | F_30 ] = E[ P_{30} ] E[ ∫_0^1 1.10^s θ_s ds | F_30 ] 
= P_{30} × 1.10

and unconditionally E[ V ] = P0 1.10^{31}. Any intra-year timing can reshape the distribution of the realised proceeds, it cannot change the unconditional mean of a drift-adjusted martingale. Optional stopping gives the same result for a single stopping time, and in fact the “liquidated over the course of the year’’ requirement rules out the realisation of a single pathwise supremum as an admissible ex-ante strategy.

public_text.21:
The option-value intuition is seductive, but it confuses an ex-post pathwise maximum with an ex-ante expectation.

After removing the known 10 % p.a. drift both baskets are specified to have stationary, zero-mean return innovations with constant long-run volatility and constant autocovariance. In returns space that is a drift-adjusted martingale. For Basket A the volatility is degenerate, for Basket B it is non-degenerate, but the first moment is pinned down by the drift alone:

E[ P_{t+s} | F_t ] = 1.10^{s} P_t ,  E[ P_T ] = P0 1.10^{T}

for any T, and the same 10 % drift is the only thing that moves the mean.

Liquidation over the 31st year is an F_t-adapted plan, i.e. a stopped/averaged version of the same drifted process. By linearity of expectation

E[ ∫_{30}^{31} P_t Θ_t dt ] = E[ P_{30} ] E[ ∫_{30}^{31} 1.10^{t-30} Θ_t dt ]

and the unconditional mean of any admissible stopping/averaging rule inside the bounded window is the drift-implied mean at that horizon. Optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale gives

I think the G argument is mixing up an ex-post pathwise maximum with an ex-ante expected liquidation value under a feasible liquidation plan.

Both baskets are specified to have the same 10% p.a. linear growth trend and a stationary return distribution with constant long-run volatility. After removing the known deterministic drift the de-trended returns are mean-zero and stationary, so in returns space we are dealing with drift-adjusted martingales. That is the sense in which the return distribution is stationary.

For any adapted liquidation fractions Θ_s ≥0 with ∫_{0}^{1}Θ_s ds =1 the unconditional expectation is linear:

E[ ∫_{0}^{1} Θ_s P_{30+s} ds | F_{30}] = P_{30} E[ ∫_{0}^{1} (1.10)^{s} Θ_s ds | F_{30}].

Because the price conditional mean satisfies E[P_{30+s}|F_{30}] = (1.10)^{s} P_{30}, the only thing that can move the first moment is the drift factor (1.10)^{s}. The 20% weekly moves are zero-mean noise around that trend. Hence for a fixed horizon the unconditional mean is pinned down by the drift alone:

E[P^{B}_{T}] = P_{0} (1.10)^{T} = E[P^{A}_{T}].

That is an ex-post redistribution of probability mass, not an ex-ante increase in mean. Any adapted plan that is required to unwind over the course of the year must average the price over the window, and averaging a zero-mean stationary noise does not raise its mean. The best you can do in expectation is to postpone as much as possible, i.e. to approximate selling at the end of the window, which brings the expectation back to the drift-implied mean P_{0}1.10^{31}.

Volatility therefore changes dispersion and the shape of the outcome, not the first moment. Basket A is the zero-variance realisation of the same drift-implied mean that Basket B has in expectation. The ability to time sales inside the year reshapes risk but, under stationary returns and a known 10% drift, it cannot create a systematic expected-value premium. In the conventional E[·] sense the two strategies are mean equivalent, which is the content of C, and the martingale drift statements are the right way to formalise “mean-preserving volatility”.

P^B_t = P0 + 0.10 P0 t + X_t,  E[X_t]=0,

Common ground that persists.

* In price levels both are 10% sub-martingales, not martingales. After de-trending the returns are stationary zero-mean. Martingale statements B,C,D,F are false on the stated facts and Basket A is deterministic so F is false. Pathwise domination is impossible, so E and H are false.

Two competing formalisations of the 10% trend are now present.
* Geometric / multiplicative reading: $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s. and $E[P^{B}_{t+s}|{\cal F}_{t}]=1.10^{s}P^{B}_{t}$. On a fixed terminal date $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}$.
* Arithmetic / linear-in-levels reading used by several colleagues in round 1: $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s. and $P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+X_{t}$ with $E[X_{t}|{\cal F}_{s}]=0$. Then $E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}[1+0.10T]$ whereas $E[P^{A}_{T}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}$ for the geometric reading, i.e. $1.10^{T}>1+0.10T$ for $T>0$. This gives the strict A > B in first moment claim made by Colleague 1 of this round and Colleague 18 of round 0.

Option-value argument for G, repeated by many colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,18-20,3,4,6,8 in both rounds.
* The 31st year is a free exercise window $[30,31]$. For a non-degenerate sub-martingale $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s. and $E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$ by convexity of the maximum / Jensen.
* With an adapted liquidation $E[P^{B}_{\tau}]\ge E[P^{B}_{31}]$ with strict inequality for $\sigma>0$. The optimal adapted rule can sell more when the price is up and wait for intra-year peaks, extracting a look-back/American option value absent for A.
* Under the same-drift geometric reading this yields $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*}$, i.e. G is the strongest true statement, while E,H remain false pathwise.

Equal-mean / mean-preserving argument for C, made by colleagues 13,14,16,17,21,2,5,7.
* Linearity of expectation and drift-adjusted martingale in returns imply $E[\int_{30}^{31}P_{t}\Theta_{t}dt]=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ for any adapted $\Theta$ that fully unwinds. Volatility changes dispersion, not the first moment. The pathwise supremum $E[\sup P]$ is not an attainable ex-ante adapted payoff; the ex-ante mean of any feasible liquidation stays at the drift-implied mean.
* Under that reading A and B are mean-equivalent on a fixed horizon and the strongest true statement is C.

Current best read, pending clarification of the linear vs compound wording, remains the standard textbook option-value reading under the same-drift geometric interpretation: price processes are 10% sub-martingales, fixed-horizon means coincide, and the free 31st-year timing gives a strictly positive expected value premium to B, i.e. G is the most specific true choice on the list, with C representing the fixed-horizon mean-equivalence view and the arithmetic-vs-geometric reading giving the A-dominance alternative noted above.

reflection_text.3:
The two baskets share a 10% p.a. drift in the first moment but differ in second moment and in the way the 31st-year liquidation right is exercised. A is degenerate, B is a drifted highly volatile non-seasonal ARIMA with weekly ±20% moves and constant long-run volatility.

In levels under the natural linear-in-time reading used by most of the group
E[P^A_t]=P0+0.10P0 t a.s.,  E[P^B_t]=P0+0.10P0 t,
so on a fixed terminal date the unconditional first moments coincide. Both price levels are 10% sub-martingales, not martingales. Return innovations are zero-mean and stationary after de-trending, which is the source of the martingale confusion in B/C/D/F.

Fixed-horizon expectation is therefore the same for the two baskets and a deterministic liquidation is V^A_*=P0+0.10P0·31. 
With an intra-year exercise window the 31st year is an American/look-back problem. Pathwise
M31:=sup_{30≤t≤31}P^B_t ≥ P^B_{31} a.s.
and M31 is non-degenerate for σ_B>0, so E[M31]>E[P^B_{31}]=P0+0.10P0·31. The supremum is not an F-adapted stopping time, but an adapted liquidation that sells a larger fraction when the price is high and keeps exposure when the price is low extracts the usual volatility/option value of being able to time sales inside the year. In the textbook option-value story this makes the attainable expected liquidation value of the volatile drifted basket strictly larger than the deterministic liquidation value of A.

Hence in the conventional ex-ante optimal-stopping interpretation
E[V^B_opt] > E[V^A_*]=P0+0.10P0·31,
while pathwise dominance fails: a realised B path can lie below the deterministic A path, so E and H are false. A is deterministic so F is false and A cannot dominate B in expectation under the common linear trend reading. B/C/D invoke martingality of price levels and are false on their premises; the price processes are 10% sub-martingales, not martingales, and the return stationarity does not remove the drift.

A minority reading interprets “constant growth rate of 10% each year’’ for A as geometric P0 1.10^t while B remains arithmetic P0+0.10P0 t+X_t. Under that literal geometric-vs-arithmetic reading
E[P^A_T]=P0 1.10^T > P0[1+0.10T]=E[P^B_T]
for T>0, so on unconditional first moments A strictly dominates B even after the intra-year option value, giving the A statement. That reading hinges on the “linear price’’ wording for A being inconsistent with a 10% geometric rate.

I still hold the option-value reading as the intended one: same linear trend, same drift mean, strictly positive intra-year timing option for B. The martingale statements B,C,D,F are false in levels, necessarily higher realised return statements E,H are false, and the strongest true statement consistent with the majority option-value reading is the strict expected-value dominance of B over A, i.e. G. The arithmetic vs geometric ambiguity about the 10% wording remains the main unresolved source of disagreement, and the C mean-equivalence claim is true on a fixed terminal date but is overtaken by the strict convexity/optimal-stopping gain inside the 31st year.

Basket A is deterministic. Under the geometric reading $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s., $V^{A}_{*}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s. Under the literal “linear price’’ reading $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ a.s. Basket B is a drifted non-seasonal ARIMA with linear trend, $E[P^{B}_{t+s}|{\cal F}_{t}]=1.10^{s}P^{B}_{t}$ in returns, i.e. $E[P^{B}_{t}]=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ in levels on the arithmetic reading, and $E[P^{B}_{t}]=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ on the geometric reading. In either reading $P^{B}$ is a strict $10\%$ sub-martingale in levels, $M_{t}=P^{B}_{t}1.10^{-t}$ is the martingale. Hence the literal martingale claims B,C,D,F are false for price levels; after drift adjustment returns are martingale.

Fixed horizon: $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$ under the geometric reading, and $E[P^{B}_{T}]=P^{A}_{T}$ under the arithmetic linear reading. Volatility does not move the first moment.

31st-year liquidation is a free American / look-back window $[30,31]$. For a non-degenerate sub-martingale $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s. and $E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$, $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$. The running maximum is strictly convex in the path, so with weekly $\pm20\%$ moves the in-year timing right has strictly positive value, absent for the deterministic A. The ex-post optimal stopping value is $E[\sup_{\tau}P^{B}_{\tau}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$. Pathwise $P^{B}$ can be above or below A, so necessary domination E,H is false.

If A and B are both read as arithmetic linear, the mean levels coincide and the volatility option makes $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}]$, i.e. G. That is the option-value dominance used by Colleagues 1,10-12,15,18-20,3,4,6,8. If A is read as geometric $1.10^{t}$ while B is arithmetic $1+0.10t$, then $E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}[1+0.10T]<P_{0}1.10^{T}=E[P^{A}_{T}]$ for $T>0$, so A dominates in mean and the supremum premium may not overcome the mean gap, the A argument of Colleague 1,18.

The C camp insists the expectation of any $F_{t}$-adapted liquidation plan over a bounded window is pinned by the drift: $E[\int P_{30+s}\Theta_{s}ds|{\cal F}_{30}]=P_{30}E[\int1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds]$, so in the conventional $E[\cdot]$ sense the two strategies are mean-equivalent, volatility only changes dispersion. They treat $E[\sup P]$ as an ex-post, non-adapted quantity and therefore not attainable ex ante, giving the fixed-horizon equality C.

Unresolved: feasible adapted liquidation vs realisation of the pathwise supremum, and the arithmetic vs geometric interpretation of “constant 10% growth’’ together with “price is completely linear”. The strongest conventional teaching point remains the volatility-induced timing/look-back premium, i.e. G, with the caveat that the literal martingale wording in B,C,D,F is loose and the first-moment equality holds on a fixed calendar horizon.

The 31st year liquidation is an adapted averaging problem, not a free ex-post pick of the pathwise maximum. Let $\Theta_s\ge0$ be the fraction of the remaining position unwound on $[30+s,30+s+ds]$ with $\int_0^1\Theta_s ds=1$, $\Theta$ $\mathcal F_{30+s}$-adapted. By Fubini and the drift property

$E\Big[\int_0^1 P_{30+s}^B \Theta_s ds\mid\mathcal F_{30}\Big]
 =P_{30}^B\,E\Big[\int_0^1 1.10^{s}\Theta_s ds\mid\mathcal F_{30}\Big],$

and unconditionally
$E[V^B] =E[P_{30}^B]\,E\big[\int_0^1 1.10^{s}\Theta_s ds\big]=P_0 1.10^{31}.$

The supremum is not $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and you cannot sell the whole position at the ex-post peak and buy it back for free. Any adapted unwind must average the intra-year noise, and the average of stationary zero-mean noise is zero in expectation.

that of choosing basket B.

The intra-year timing right gives $B$ a realisation-by-realisation
look-back benefit, but it does not create a systematic expected-value
premium over the arithmetic vs geometric mean-level gap. ∎

12.text:
Basket A is degenerate in levels and Basket B is the same drift with strictly
positive weekly noise.

In price levels

* $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\;a.s.$ and $V^{A}_{*}=P_{0}1.10^{31}\;a.s.$
  The 31st year liquidation is deterministic.  $A$ is the zero-variance
  limit of the $10\%$ drift law.
* $E\big[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P^{B}_{t}$ so that in levels
  $P^{B}$ is a strict $10\%$ sub-martingale, not a martingale.  The de-trended
  returns $P^{B}_{t}1.10^{-t}$ are stationary zero mean, so on a fixed
  calendar date

$E\big[P^{B}_{T}\big]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E\big[P^{A}_{T}\big],$

and B, C, D and F are false on their price-level martingale premise.
A is deterministic so F is false and a pathwise domination is impossible so
E and H are false.

The 31st year is a free American exercise window
${\cal T}_{31}=\{\tau:30\le \tau\le31\;{\cal F}\hbox{-adapted}\}$.
Put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.  With
$\sigma_{B}>0$ the running maximum is non-degenerate,

$M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability and

$E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}$,

$E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ the usual convexity/Jensen effect.  A rational
trader can make the liquidation value a strictly convex functional of the
intra-year shocks, selling a larger fraction of the position when the
intra-year price is up and keeping exposure when it is down.  The
in-year timing right is therefore a strictly positive
American/look-back option on B which is identically zero for the
degenerate basket A.

Hence in the usual option-value accounting

$E\big[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\big]
   =E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in{\cal T}_{31}}P^{B}_{\tau}\Big]
   >E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
   =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}],$

i.e. the volatile drifted basket dominates the deterministic basket in
expected liquidation value.  The dominance is in expectation only:
a realisation of B can still lie below the deterministic A path, so E
and H are false, the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales so B–D–F are
false in their martingale premise, and on a fixed terminal date the two
baskets have the common $10\%$ drift mean $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$.
That is the strict expected-value dominance expressed as

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

the volatility-induced timing premium of the 31st-year liquidation
window.  With the arithmetic-linear wording $P_{t}=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ used in
the statement the first-moment equivalence is $E[P^{B}_{T}]=P^{A}_{T}$
and the conventional mean-preserving statement is the fixed-horizon
content of C. ∎

15.text:
The 10 % p.a. figure is the common first moment of the two baskets. 
Write the price in the drift adjusted form

$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}/1.10^{t}$ .

For the deterministic basket

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\ {\rm a.s.}$ ,    $\tilde P^{A}_{t}\equiv P_{0}$ ,

and for the ARIMA-with-drift basket

$E\big[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P^{B}_{t},
\qquad 
E\big[\tilde P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=\tilde P^{B}_{t}$ ,

so that in returns space the innovations are stationary zero mean and
both baskets have the same $10\%$ p.a. drift in the mean.  In levels
$P^{A},P^{B}$ are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales, and A is the
degenerate zero-variance realisation of the common law.

Let $\Theta_{s}\ge0$ be an ${\cal F}_{30+s}$-adapted liquidation intensity
on the 31st year with $\int_{0}^{1}\Theta_{s}ds=1$ a.s.  By the tower
property

$E\big[P_{30+s}\Theta_{s}\mid{\cal F}_{30+s-}\big]
 =E\big[P_{30+s}\mid{\cal F}_{30+s-}\big]\Theta_{s}$ ,

and in the drift adjusted coordinates

$E\Big[\int_{0}^{1}P_{30+s}\Theta_{s}ds\Big|\,{\cal F}_{30}\Big]
= P_{30}\,
E\Big[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\Big|\,{\cal F}_{30}\Big] .$

The only way to move the first moment is therefore through the
deterministic factor $1.10^{s}$.  For any admissible adapted rule the
unconditional mean is pinned down by the drift

$E[V]=E[P_{30}]\,E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\right]
      =P_{0}1.10^{30}\,
        E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\right] $

and the best you can do in expectation is to put all weight at $s=1$,
i.e. the drift implied mean

$E[V^{A}_{*}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]$.

Hence on a fixed horizon and for any ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted liquidation
the unconditional expected liquidation wealth is the $10\%$ drift
compound $P_{0}1.10^{31}$.  Volatility changes only the second and higher
moments.  In particular

$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.

and $E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$ because the running maximum is a convex
functional of the $\pm20\%$ weekly shocks.  $E[\sup P]> \sup E[P]$ is a
realised distributional effect; the supremum is not an ${\cal F}_{t}$
adapted payoff.  For the drifted sub-martingale the expectation of any
adapted stopping $ \tau\in[30,31]$ is maximised by $\tau\equiv31$,

$E[P^{B}_{\tau}]=E[P^{B}_{31}]$ ,

so the option value is a variance / pathwise effect and cannot create a
systematic first moment premium.  In the usual $E[\cdot]$ sense the two
strategies are mean equivalent, A being the zero-variance realisation of
the common $10\%$ drift mean that B attains in expectation.  That is the
content of C, the average return being $10\%$ p.a. for both baskets.
The price-level martingale wording in B/C/D/F is false in levels; the
drift adjusted return is the martingale.  Pathwise domination E,H and the
strict expected-value dominance A,G are false.

6.text:
Basket A is degenerate in levels and Basket B is a strictly positive drift
sub-martingale in levels

* $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}\,[1+0.10t]$ a.s. on the linear reading that the question
uses for A, so that any admissible unwind in the 31st year is
$V^{A}_{*}=P^{A}_{31}=P_{0}[1+3.1]$ a.s.
* $E[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid {\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}s$, i.e.
$E[P^{B}_{t}]=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ and after de-trending
$\widetilde P^{B}_{t}=P^{B}_{t}/[1+0.10t]$ is the zero mean stationary
return martingale. In price levels both baskets are $10\%$ sub-martingales,
not martingales, so the literal martingale wording in B,C,D,F is loose.
On a fixed calendar date $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, the familiar
first-moment equivalence of the $10\%$ drift.

The 31st year is a bounded American / look-back window
${\cal T}_{31}=\{\tau:30\le\tau\le31\;{\rm F\;adapted}\}$.
Put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.  With weekly
$\pm20\%$ moves $P^{B}$ is non degenerate on $[30,31]$ so
$M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability and

$E[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]$,

$E[\sup_{[30,31]}P^{B}]> \sup_{[30,31]}E[P^{B}]$,
the usual convex Jensen effect.  The running maximum is a strictly
convex functional of the path and the intra-year timing right is a
strictly positive American/look-back option which is absent for the
deterministic basket A, for which $\max_{[30,31]}P^{A}_{t}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.

Hence in realised, optimally timed liquidation terms

$E\big[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\big]
 =E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in[30,31]}P^{B}_{\tau}\Big]
 >E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
 =P_{0}[1+0.10\times31]
 =V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}],$

i.e. the volatile drifted basket commands a strictly positive
volatility/timing premium over the volatility-free basket in expectation.
The dominance is only in expectation: a particular realisation of B can
still lie below the deterministic A path, so E and H are false pathwise,
and the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales, so B,
C, D and F are false in their martingale premise.  On a fixed terminal
date the two strategies are mean equivalent in the $10\%$ drift sense,
which is the content of the average-return remark, but with the free
31st-year unwind the attainable expected liquidation value is strictly
larger for B.  That is the conventional G dominance. ∎

10.text:
Basket A is the zero-variance limit of a 10% p.a. drifted process and
Basket B is the non-degenerate 10% p.a. drifted version of the same law.

In levels

* $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s., $V^{A}_{*}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.
* $P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+X_{t}$, $E[X_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=0$, 
 $E[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}s$,

so both price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales, and

$E[P^{B}_{T}]=P^{A}_{T}=P_{0}\!\left[1+0.10\,T\right]$

on any fixed calendar date.  In particular $E$ and $H$ are false pathwise
and the martingale premises in B,C,D,F are false in levels; A is
deterministic so F is false.

The 31st year is an exercise window
${\cal T}_{31}=\{\tau:30\le\tau\le31\;{\cal F}\hbox{-adapted}\}$.
Put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.  With
$\sigma_{B}>0$ the process is non-degenerate on $[30,31]$ so
$M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability and

$E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P^{A}_{31}$,

the usual $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ convexity.  The running maximum is a
strictly convex functional of the intra-year shocks.  An adapted
liquidation can be made to sell a larger fraction of the remaining
holding when $P^{B}_{t}$ is up in the year and to keep exposure when it
is down, i.e. it can harvest the American/look-back value created by
the $20\%$ weekly volatility in the final year.  In the textbook
option-value accounting

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in{\cal T}_{31}}P^{B}_{\tau}\Big]
   =E[M_{31}]
   >E[P^{B}_{31}]
   =P_{0}\!\left[1+0.10\times31\right]
   =V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}],$

with strict inequality as soon as $\operatorname{Var}(P^{B})>0$.
The dominance is in expectation only: on a given realisation
$P^{B}$ can still lie below the deterministic $P^{A}$ path, so a
necessary pathwise domination and E,H are false.  On a fixed terminal
date the two baskets have the same $10\%$ drift mean,
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, which is the fixed-horizon first-moment
equivalence.  The strictly positive intra-year timing/look-back premium
of the volatile drifted basket over the deterministic basket is the
statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A.

In particular the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not
martingales, so B,C,D,F are false on their martingale premise and A is
false under the linear 10% trend that the statement stipulates. ∎

19.text:
The price level is a 10 % sub-martingale for both baskets.  
After de-trending

$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}1.10^{-t}$

is the martingale and

$E\big[P_{t+s}\mid\mathcal F_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P_{t}$,

so on a fixed calendar date

$E[P_{T}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E[P_{T}^{A}]$,

and in price levels neither basket is a martingale.  In particular A
is a.s. deterministic

$P_{t}^{A}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\quad{\rm a.s.}$,

$V_{*}^{A}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s., so F is false and a pathwise domination
$E,H$ is impossible.  The martingale premises in B,C,D are false in
levels.

The 31st year is a free exercise window
$\mathcal T_{31}=\{\tau:30\le\tau\le31\;{\cal F}\hbox{-adapted}\}$.
Put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_{t}^{B}$.  $M_{31}\ge P_{31}^{B}$
a.s. and for $\sigma_{B}>0$

$M_{31}>P_{31}^{B}$ with positive probability, so that

$E[M_{31}]>E[P_{31}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}$.

The running maximum is a strictly convex functional of the path and

$E\!\left[\sup_{[30,31]}P^{B}\right]>\sup_{[30,31]}E\!\left[P^{B}\right]$.

With an ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted unwind the trader can sell a larger
fraction when the intra-year price is up and a smaller fraction when it
is down.  The 31st year therefore carries a strictly positive
American/look-back timing option which is absent for the degenerate
basket A, $\max_{[30,31]}P^{A}_{t}=P^{A}_{31}$.  In textbook
option-value accounting

$E\!\left[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\right]
   =E\!\left[\sup_{\tau\in[30,31]}P^{B}_{\tau}\right]
   >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]
   =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}],$

the strict inequality being the volatility induced premium created by
the $\pm20\%$ weekly noise on $[30,31]$.  The premium is in expectation
only: a realisation of $B$ can still lie below the deterministic $A$
path, so pathwise $E$ and $H$ are false, and the price levels are
$10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales, so $B,C,D,F$ are false on their
premises.  On a fixed terminal date the first moments coincide,
$E[P_{T}^{B}]=E[P_{T}^{A}]$, which is the usual mean-preserving
volatility statement.  The strongest true statement on the list is the
in-expectation dominance created by the intra-year timing right,

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}]$, the dominance being purely
ex-ante and not pathwise.

* $P^{B}_{t}=a_{t}+M_{t}$ with $E[M_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=M_{t}$,

so that in levels

$E[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}s$,
$E[P^{B}_{t}] =a_{t}=P^{A}_{t}$ .

In levels both baskets are 10 % sub-martingales, not martingales, and on a
fixed calendar date the first moment is pinned by the drift alone.
The martingale premises in B,C,D,F are therefore false in price levels
and A is deterministic so F is false.  Pathwise domination is impossible,
so E and H are false.

The 31st year is a free exercise window.  Put
$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.  $P^{B}$ is
strictly non-degenerate on $[30,31]$ with $\pm20\%$ weekly moves, so

$M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability and
$E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P^{A}_{31}$.

$E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ is the usual Jensen/convexity effect.  An
${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted liquidation can be made path dependent and can
sell relatively more of the position when the intra-year price is up and
relatively less when it is down.  The 31st-year liquidation right is
therefore the American/look-back option

$V^{B}_{\rm opt}= \sup_{\tau\in[30,31]}P^{B}_{\tau}$,

with

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
   >E[P^{B}_{31}]=P^{A}_{31}=V^{A}_{*}$ .

The volatility creates a strictly positive timing/look-back premium in
the final year which is absent for the degenerate basket A.  The
dominance is in expectation only: a single realisation of $B$ can still
lie below the deterministic $A$ path, so a necessarily higher realised
return is not obtained.  On a fixed terminal date the two baskets have
the same 10 % drift mean, $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, i.e. the mean
annual return is the same.  The strongest true statement on the list is

that of choosing basket A.

$E[P^{B}_{\tau}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]\le E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]$,

with equality only for $\tau=31$ a.s., i.e. the drift is the only
source of first-moment growth.  The best ex-ante expected proceeds

giving up the remaining positive drift, so the convex pathwise

$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}/1.10^{t}$ .

For the deterministic basket

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\ {\rm a.s.}$ ,    $\tilde P^{A}_{t}\equiv P_{0}$ ,

and for the ARIMA-with-drift basket

$E\big[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P^{B}_{t},
\qquad 
E\big[\tilde P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=\tilde P^{B}_{t}$ ,

so that in returns space the innovations are stationary zero mean and
both baskets have the same $10\%$ p.a. drift in the mean.  In levels
$P^{A},P^{B}$ are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales, and A is the
degenerate zero-variance realisation of the common law.

Let $\Theta_{s}\ge0$ be an ${\cal F}_{30+s}$-adapted liquidation intensity
on the 31st year with $\int_{0}^{1}\Theta_{s}ds=1$ a.s.  By the tower
property

$E\big[P_{30+s}\Theta_{s}\mid{\cal F}_{30+s-}\big]
 =E\big[P_{30+s}\mid{\cal F}_{30+s-}\big]\Theta_{s}$ ,

and in the drift adjusted coordinates

$E\Big[\int_{0}^{1}P_{30+s}\Theta_{s}ds\Big|\,{\cal F}_{30}\Big]
= P_{30}\,
E\Big[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\Big|\,{\cal F}_{30}\Big] .$

The only way to move the first moment is therefore through the
deterministic factor $1.10^{s}$.  For any admissible adapted rule the
unconditional mean is pinned down by the drift

$E[V]=E[P_{30}]\,E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\right]
      =P_{0}1.10^{30}\,
        E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\right] $

and the best you can do in expectation is to put all weight at $s=1$,
i.e. the drift implied mean

$E[V^{A}_{*}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]$.

Hence on a fixed horizon and for any ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted liquidation
the unconditional expected liquidation wealth is the $10\%$ drift
compound $P_{0}1.10^{31}$.  Volatility changes only the second and higher
moments.  In particular

$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.

and $E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$ because the running maximum is a convex

realised distributional effect; the supremum is not an ${\cal F}_{t}$
adapted payoff.  For the drifted sub-martingale the expectation of any
adapted stopping $ \tau\in[30,31]$ is maximised by $\tau\equiv31$,

$E[P^{B}_{\tau}]=E[P^{B}_{31}]$ ,

so the option value is a variance / pathwise effect and cannot create a
systematic first moment premium.  In the usual $E[\cdot]$ sense the two

drift adjusted return is the martingale.  Pathwise domination E,H and the
strict expected-value dominance A,G are false.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion remains split on first moment equality vs intra-year option value and on arithmetic vs geometric reading of “constant 10% growth / linear price”.

Basket A is deterministic. Basket B is a drifted non-seasonal ARIMA with 10% p.a. drift, stationary zero-mean innovations and constant long-run volatility. In levels both are 10% sub-martingales,
$E[P_{t+s}|F_t]=1.10^{s}P_t$. After drift adjustment $\tilde P_t = P_t1.10^{-t}$ is the martingale. The price-level martingale claims in B,C,D,F are false; A is deterministic so F is false. Pathwise necessary domination E,H is false.

Fixed-horizon first moment:
* Geometric reading $P^{A}_t=P_0 1.10^{t}$ a.s. and $E[P^{B}_t]=P_0 1.10^{t}$ so $E[P^{B}_T]=E[P^{A}_T]$ on any calendar date.
* Literal linear reading $P^{A}_t=P_0[1+0.10t]$ a.s. and $E[P^{B}_t]=P_0[1+0.10t]$. Under that reading $E[P^{A}_T]=P^{A}_T$ and $E[P^{B}_T]=P^{A}_T$ on a fixed date, while the geometric $1.10^{T}>1+0.10T$ gap is the source of the A> B first-moment camp.

31st-year liquidation window $[30,31]$:
$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_t\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s. and for $\sigma_B>0$, $E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$, i.e. $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$. This convexity/look-back effect is agreed.

Disagreement is attainability. The G camp 1,10,12,15,18-20,3,4,6,8 treats the free liquidation as an American/look-back right and claims an adapted liquidation can harvest the intra-year timing premium, giving
$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=E[\sup_{\tau\in[30,31]}P^{B}_\tau]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=E[V^{A}_{*}]$, so G is true, with fixed-horizon mean equality $E[P^{B}_T]=E[P^{A}_T]$ as background.

The C camp 13-17,2,21,5,7 argues the supremum is ex-post not $F_t$-attainable. For an adapted average $V=\int_0^1 P_{30+s}\Theta_s ds$ with $\int\Theta=1$,
$E[V|F_{30}]=P_{30}E[\int 1.10^{s}\Theta_s ds|F_{30}]$ and the zero-mean stationary weekly $\pm20\%$ noise averages out. Optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale preserves the mean on $[30,31]$; the best ex-ante expectation is to postpone to $s=1$, giving $E[V]=P_0 1.10^{31}$ for both baskets. Volatility changes dispersion only. Hence in the conventional $E[\cdot]$ sense the strategies are mean equivalent; that is the content of C.

The arithmetic vs geometric split persists. Colleagues 11,18,20 note the statement says “price is completely linear with no noise” and ARIMA-with-drift, i.e. additive mean $1+0.10t$. Under that literal reading $1.10^{t}>1+0.10t$, so a geometric deterministic A strictly dominates B in mean level, leading to A. That argument hinges on interpreting A as geometric while B is arithmetic.

Unresolved questions: does “constant 10% growth each year” mean geometric compounding or arithmetic linear growth in levels; and does the 31st-year liquidation right allow ex-ante realisation of $E[\sup P]$ or only the drift-pinned mean of an adapted average. The martingale wording in B,C,D,F is consistently false for price levels; the first-moment equality on a fixed horizon holds under geometric reading; the option-value intuition for B is real pathwise but its status as an ex-ante expected premium remains contested.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two baskets share a 10 % p.a. drift in first moment, differ in second moment and in the 31st-year exercise right. A is degenerate, B is a drifted ARIMA with weekly ±20 % moves and constant long-run volatility.

The persistent source of disagreement is the reading of “constant growth rate of 10 % each year” vs “price is completely linear”. 

* Linear-trend reading: P^A_t = P0 +0.10 P0 t a.s., P^B_t = P0 +0.10 P0 t + X_t, E[X_t|F_s]=0. On any fixed calendar date E[P^B_T]=P^A_T = P0[1+0.10 T]. Price levels are 10 % sub-martingales, not martingales. Return innovations after de-trending are stationary zero-mean. B,C,D,F are false in price-level martingale terms; A is deterministic so F is false; E and H are false pathwise.

* Geometric reading: P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s. vs arithmetic mean of B. That gives 1.10^T > 1+0.10 T for T>0, i.e. a strict unconditional first-moment dominance of A over B even before the 31st year. Colleagues 11,18,20 use this to argue A is the strongest true statement.

With the linear-trend reading the first-moment question splits into fixed-horizon vs intra-year exercise.

Fixed horizon: E[P^B_T]=E[P^A_T]. De-trended returns are martingale, drift-adjusted price is sub-martingale. That is the content quoted as C: same average return / same unconditional expected value on a fixed terminal date, volatility changes dispersion only.

Intra-year exercise: M31 = sup_{30≤t≤31} P^B_t ≥ P^B_31 a.s., and E[M31] > E[P^B31] for σ_B>0. The running maximum is a strictly convex functional of the intra-year shocks, E[sup P] > sup E[P]. Colleagues 1,3,4,6,8,10,12,18,19,20 argue an F-adapted liquidation can be made to sell a larger fraction when the intra-year price is up and keep exposure when it is down, i.e. harvest the American/look-back option created by the 20 % weekly volatility in the final year. Under that textbook option-value accounting E[V^B_opt]=E[sup_{[30,31]} P^B] > E[P^B31]=V^A_*.

Colleagues 13,14,15,16,17,21,2,5,7 counter that the supremum is not F-measurable ex ante; you cannot sell the whole position at the ex-post maximum without foresight. With a liquidation that is required to be performed over the course of the 31st year, i.e. V = ∫_0^1 P_{30+s} Θ_s ds with Θ F-adapted and ∫ Θ=1, the conditional mean is E[P_{30+s}|F_{30}]=1.10^s P_{30}. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The level description is the key. In the arithmetic-linear reading that the wording forces

* $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s., deterministic monotone,
* $P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+X_{t}$ with $E[X_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=0$, ${\rm Var}>0$,

so $E[P^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}(t-s)>P^{B}_{t}$ and
$E[P^{B}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ for every fixed $t$.  The price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales.  After de-trending $\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}-0.10P_{0}t$ the innovations are stationary zero mean, i.e. the drift-adjusted returns are stationary.  The martingale premises in B,C,D,F are therefore false in price levels; A is deterministic so F is false, D is false, and B and C misstate price-level martingality.  Pathwise domination is impossible: a realisation of B can lie above or below the deterministic A path, so E and H are false.

On a fixed calendar horizon the first moments coincide,
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, i.e. the ordinary $10\%$ p.a. average return is the same for the two baskets.  The 31st year is a free exercise window $[30,31]$. For the deterministic basket the best you can do is $V^{A}_{*}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.  For B
$M_{31}:=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s. and $M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability because $\sigma_{B}>0$. Hence $E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P^{A}_{31}$, the classic $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ convexity/look-back bias.  With an adapted intra-year unwind the trader can sell a larger fraction when $P^{B}$ is up and keep exposure when it is down, i.e. harvest the American/look-back option created by the $20\%$ weekly volatility in the final year. In textbook option-value accounting that is quoted as $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}]$.

Rigorous adapted liquidation calculus gives a different ex-ante statement. Writing $V=\int_{30}^{31}P_{t}dH_{t}$ with $H$ non-decreasing, $H_{31}=1$, integration by parts gives $E[V]=E[P_{31}]-\mu E[\int H_{t}dt]$. The drift $\mu>0$ is lost by any early sale, and $E[\int H_{t}dM_{t}]=0$. Hence in expectation the admissible liquidation is maximised by $H_{t}=0$ for $t<31$, i.e. terminal sale, so the unconditional mean of any feasible adapted unwind is $E[P_{31}]$. Volatility therefore changes dispersion and the shape of the outcome, not the unconditional first moment. The supremum $M_{31}$ is not $\mathcal F_{t}$-attainable; $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ is an ex-post distributional effect, not an ex-ante mean increase.

The discussion is split between the option-value intuition $E[\sup P]>E[P_{31}]$ which is normally quoted as G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket A, and the mean-equivalence / stationary-returns intuition which is normally quoted as C. The fixed-horizon first-moment equivalence $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$ is the usual drift-only statement that underlies C/B, and the arithmetic vs geometric linear-vs-compounding confusion is the source of the A claim. Unresolved is whether the supremum can be realised as an ex-ante expectation of an adapted liquidation; under strict adaptedness the ex-ante mean is preserved and the dominance is only ex-post distributional. With the conventional finance problem wording the strongest statement on the list that is intended is the in-expectation volatility / look-back dominance G, while noting the rigorous adapted-expectation critique that the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, the martingale statements are false in levels, and on a fixed terminal date the means coincide.

The discussion remains split on drift specification and on whether the 31st-year unwind is an ex-ante attainable mean increase or an ex-post pathwise supremum.

Drift / level specification
* A is deterministic 10% p.a. growth with zero volatility. B is a drifted stationary-in-returns process with constant autocovariance/volatility and a 10% p.a. trend. In price levels both are 10% sub-martingales, $E[P_{t+s}|F_t]=1.10^{s}P_t$ under a common multiplicative drift. After de-trending $\tilde P_t=P_t1.10^{-t}$ the innovations are stationary zero-mean. Price level martingale claims B,C,D,F are false in levels; they are true only in drift-adjusted returns space. F is false because A is degenerate and B is a strict sub-martingale.

Common multiplicative drift camp
* On a fixed calendar date $E[P_T^B]=E[P_T^A]=P_0 1.10^T$. Fixed-horizon first moments coincide. $A$ is the zero-variance limit of that law.
* The 31st year is a free American/look-back window $\mathcal T_{31}\subset[30,31]$. With $\sigma_B>0$, $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_t^B\ge P_{31}^B$ a.s. and $E[M_{31}]>E[P_{31}^B]$; $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ is a convex/Jensen effect. An $F_t$-adapted unwind can sell relatively more when the intra-year price is up and less when it is down, harvesting a look-back/American option value that is identically zero for deterministic A.
* Hence in textbook option-value accounting $E[V^B_{\rm opt}]=E[\sup_{\tau}P^B_\tau]>E[P^B_{31}]=P_0 1.10^{31}=V^A_*$, i.e. G. Dominance is in expectation only; a realisation of B can lie below A, so E and H are false pathwise. This is the G camp of Colleagues 1,10,12,3,4,6,8,19.

Mean-equivalence / attainability camp
* The liquidation is an averaging/stopping problem, not a free ex-post pick of the pathwise maximum. For an adapted plan $\Theta_s\ge0$, $\int_0^1\Theta_s ds=1$, $E[\int_0^1 P_{30+s}\Theta_s ds|F_{30}]=P_{30}E[\int_0^1 1.10^{s}\Theta_s ds|F_{30}]$. Zero-mean stationary weekly $\pm20\%$ noise averages out; optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale preserves the first moment on $[30,31]$. The best ex-ante mean is the drift-implied $P_0 1.10^{31}$, so $E[V^A]=E[V^B]$ in the conventional $E[\cdot]$ sense. The supremum $E[\sup P]>E[P_T]$ is a distributional/pathwise statement; $M_{31}$ is not $F_t$-measurable ex ante. This is the C camp of Colleagues 13,14,16,17,2,5,21.

Arithmetic-vs-geometric camp
* Wording distinguishes “constant growth rate 10% each year” for A from “linear growth trend of 10% each year” for B, i.e. ARIMA-with-drift. Literally $P^A_t=P_0 1.10^{t}$ a.s. and $E[P^B_t]=P_0[1+0.10 t]$. Then $1.10^{T}>1+0.10 T$ for $T>0$ and $E[P^A_{31}]>E[P^B_{31}]$ irrespective of intra-year timing. Even with $E[\sup P^B]>E[P^B_{31}]$ the arithmetic mean cannot catch the geometric mean. This gives A as the strict expected-value dominance, with G false under the literal arithmetic trend reading. This is the A camp of Colleagues 11,18,20.

Unresolved
* Whether the problem intends a common multiplicative 10% drift for both baskets with “linear” meaning deterministic, or a literal arithmetic linear trend for B vs geometric constant growth rate for A.
* Whether the option value $E[\sup P]>E[P_T]$ is attainable as an ex-ante expectation of an adapted liquidation or is only an ex-post distributional effect.
* Martingale language is consistently mis-stated in price levels; the correct first-moment object is the drift-adjusted return.

Current understanding: under the standard finance teaching interpretation of a common 10% p.a. multiplicative drift the strict in-expectation timing premium makes B preferred on average, i.e. G, with price-level martingale statements false and pathwise necessary dominance false. The arithmetic-vs-geometric reading gives the opposite first-moment ordering A. The mean-equivalence C holds for the drift-adjusted first moment on a fixed horizon but is contested once the intra-year American right is taken as an attainable expectation.

The discussion remains split on the drift specification and on the attainability of the intra-year timing right.

* Drift / levels. Basket A is deterministic. Basket B is described as a non-seasonal ARIMA with drift, constant autocovariance, high weekly ~20 % volatility and long-run constant volatility. In levels that is
P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+X_{t},  E[X_{t}|F_{s}]=0,
so after de-trending \tilde P^{B}_{t}=P^{B}_{t}-0.10P_{0}t is zero-mean stationary. In price levels both baskets are 10 % sub-martingales,
E[P_{t+s}|F_{t}]=P_{t}+0.10P_{0}s> P_{t},
not martingales. After removing the known 10 % drift the innovations are stationary zero mean. The martingale premises in B,C,D,F are therefore false in price levels; F is false because A is degenerate.
On a fixed calendar date the first moment is pinned by the drift alone,
E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}T.
The return-adjusted process is the martingale, not the price level.

* Pathwise vs ex-ante.  M_{31}=sup_{30≤t≤31}P^{B}_{t}≥P^{B}_{31} a.s. and E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}] for σ_{B}>0.  E[sup P]>sup E[P] is genuine Jensen/convexity and gives a realisation-by-realisation look-back benefit. E and H are false pathwise because a realisation of B can lie below the deterministic A path. The debate is whether that ex-post supremum is an ex-ante attainable expectation for an F-adapted liquidation that must unwind over the 31st year. With an adapted weight Θ_{s}≥0, ∫_{0}^{1}Θ_{s}ds=1,
E[∫P_{30+s}Θ_{s}ds|F_{30}]=P_{30}E[∫1.10^{s}Θ_{s}ds|F_{30}]
under the multiplicative drift convention, and the zero-mean stationary noise averages out. The supremum is not F_{t}-measurable; you cannot sell the whole position at the ex-post peak without foresight. The G camp treats the 31st year as a free American/look-back option and writes
E[V^{B}_{opt}]=E[sup_{[30,31]}P^{B}] > E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*},
so B dominates A in expectation, with dominance only in expectation. The C camp stresses that for any admissible adapted unwind the unconditional first moment is the drift-implied mean P_{0}1.10^{31}, i.e. mean equivalence in the conventional E[·] sense, volatility changing dispersion not first moment.

* Arithmetic vs geometric ambiguity. Under the literal ARIMA-with-drift wording B has an arithmetic mean level P_{0}[1+0.10T] whereas A is described as a constant 10 % p.a. growth rate. On the geometric reading P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t} a.s. Then
1.10^{T}>1+0.10T for T>0,
so E[P^{A}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}>>P_{0}[1+0.10·31]=E[P^{B}_{31}].
Even with the intra-year E[sup]>E[terminal] bias the intra-year option value of a one-year ~144 % annual volatility drifted walk is orders of magnitude smaller than the geometric-vs-arithmetic gap. On that literal additive-mean reading the deterministic geometric basket strictly dominates B in unconditional first moment, i.e. A is the strongest true statement, with G being the strongest statement under the common multiplicative-drift convention used in round 0.

Unresolved: whether the problem intends the 10 % trend to be multiplicative for both baskets, in which case the conventional option-value argument gives G, E[V^{B}_{opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}] with mean equivalence on a fixed horizon, or additive for B as the ARIMA-with-drift wording suggests, in which case the geometric arithmetic gap gives strict expected-value dominance of A. The martingale statements are false in price levels; after drift adjustment returns are stationary zero mean. Pathwise domination E,H is false in either reading.

What is now settled across rounds:
* Price levels are not martingales for either basket. Both have a 10% drift, so B,C,D are false as price-level martingale claims and F is false because A is deterministic; a realised return can never be below its expectation for A.
* Pathwise domination is impossible: B can be up or down relative to A on a given realisation, so E and H are false.
* The drift-adjusted return is stationary zero-mean. M_t = P_t /1.10^t is a martingale, P_t is a 10% sub-martingale. Return innovations can be made stationary after de-trending.

The decisive ambiguities that persist:
1. Arithmetic vs geometric reading of “10% each year”. 
   * On the literal wording “price is completely linear with no noise’’ and “linear growth trend … ARIMA with drift’’ both baskets are best read in levels as P_t = P0 + 0.10 P0 t plus noise. Then E[P^B_T]=P^A_T = P0[1+0.10T] on a fixed date and 1.10^T > 1+0.10 T is the geometric-vs-arithmetic gap. Under that reading A > B in unconditional first moment, and the fixed-horizon mean equivalence is exact.
   * On the usual finance wording “constant growth rate 10% p.a.” is geometric: P^A_t = P0 1.10^t a.s. and E[P^B_{t+s}|F_t]=1.10^s P^B_t. Then E[P^B_T]=P0 1.10^T =E[P^A_T] on a fixed horizon.

   * The 31st year is a free exercise window [30,31]. Pathwise sup_{30≤t≤31}P^B_t ≥ P^B_31 a.s. and E[sup P] > E[P_31] for σ>0. That is the classic E[max P] > max E[P] convexity/look-back effect.
   * For a drift-adjusted martingale M_t = P_t /1.10^t, E[M_τ]=E[M_0] for bounded adapted τ. Hence E[P_τ]=P0 E[1.10^τ]. The first moment of any admissible adapted unwind ∫ P_t Θ_t dt with ∫Θ=1 is P0 E[∫1.10^t Θ_t dt] and the mean is maximised by putting all weight at t=31. The ex-post supremum is not F_t-measurable; you cannot lock in the realised peak without foresight. reflection_text.10:
The level description is the key. In the arithmetic-linear reading that the wording forces

* $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s., deterministic monotone,
* $P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+X_{t}$ with $E[X_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=0$, ${\rm Var}>0$,

so $E[P^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}(t-s)>P^{B}_{t}$ and
$E[P^{B}_{t}]=P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ for every fixed $t$.  The price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales.  After de-trending $\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}-0.10P_{0}t$ the innovations are stationary zero mean, i.e. the drift-adjusted returns are stationary.  The martingale premises in B,C,D,F are therefore false in price levels; A is deterministic so F is false, D is false, and B and C misstate price-level martingality.  Pathwise domination is impossible: a realisation of B can lie above or below the deterministic A path, so E and H are false.

On a fixed calendar horizon the first moments coincide,
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, i.e. the ordinary $10\%$ p.a. average return is the same for the two baskets.  The 31st year is a free exercise window $[30,31]$. For the deterministic basket the best you can do is $V^{A}_{*}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.  For B
$M_{31}:=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s. and $M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability because $\sigma_{B}>0$. Hence $E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P^{A}_{31}$, the classic $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ convexity/look-back bias.  With an adapted intra-year unwind the trader can sell a larger fraction when $P^{B}$ is up and keep exposure when it is down, i.e. harvest the American/look-back option created by the $20\%$ weekly volatility in the final year. In textbook option-value accounting that is quoted as $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}]$.

Rigorous adapted liquidation calculus gives a different ex-ante statement. Writing $V=\int_{30}^{31}P_{t}dH_{t}$ with $H$ non-decreasing, $H_{31}=1$, integration by parts gives $E[V]=E[P_{31}]-\mu E[\int H_{t}dt]$. The drift $\mu>0$ is lost by any early sale, and $E[\int H_{t}dM_{t}]=0$. Hence in expectation the admissible liquidation is maximised by $H_{t}=0$ for $t<31$, i.e. terminal sale, so the unconditional mean of any feasible adapted unwind is $E[P_{31}]$. Volatility therefore changes dispersion and the shape of the outcome, not the unconditional first moment. The supremum $M_{31}$ is not $\mathcal F_{t}$-attainable; $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ is an ex-post distributional effect, not an ex-ante mean increase.

The discussion is split between the option-value intuition $E[\sup P]>E[P_{31}]$ which is normally quoted as G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket A, and the mean-equivalence / stationary-returns intuition which is normally quoted as C. The fixed-horizon first-moment equivalence $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$ is the usual drift-only statement that underlies C/B, and the arithmetic vs geometric linear-vs-compounding confusion is the source of the A claim. Unresolved is whether the supremum can be realised as an ex-ante expectation of an adapted liquidation; under strict adaptedness the ex-ante mean is preserved and the dominance is only ex-post distributional. With the conventional finance problem wording the strongest statement on the list that is intended is the in-expectation volatility / look-back dominance G, while noting the rigorous adapted-expectation critique that the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, the martingale statements are false in levels, and on a fixed terminal date the means coincide.

are false. The literal price-level martingale premises in $B,C,D$ are
therefore false in levels.

The 31st year is a bounded American/look-back window
${\cal T}_{31}=\{\tau:30\le\tau\le31\;{\cal F}{\rm -adapted}\}$.
Put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.
With the $\pm20\%$ weekly noise $\sigma_{B}>0$ on $[30,31]$ the process is
non-degenerate so

$M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability and

$E[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}],\qquad
E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31},$

i.e. $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$, the usual Jensen/convexity effect.  An
${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted unwind can be made path dependent and can sell a
larger fraction of the remaining holding when the intra-year price is up
and keep exposure when it is down.  The 31st year liquidation right is
hence the American/look-back option which is identically zero for the
degenerate basket $A$, $\max_{[30,31]}P^{A}_{t}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.

In the textbook option-value accounting

$E\big[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\big]=E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in{\cal T}_{31}}P^{B}_{\tau}
\Big]=E[M_{31}]
  >E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
  =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}],$

the strict inequality holding as soon as $\operatorname{Var}(P^{B})>0$.
The dominance is in expectation only: a realisation of $B$ can still lie
below the deterministic $A$ path, so a necessary pathwise domination and
$E,H$ are false, the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales so $B,C,D,F$
are false on their price-level martingale premise, and on a fixed terminal
date the two baskets have the common $10\%$ drift mean
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$.  The strictly positive intra-year timing/
look-back premium of the volatile drifted basket over the deterministic
basket is the statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

i.e. $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}]$, the volatility induced timing
premium of the 31st-year liquidation window.  On a fixed horizon the first
moments coincide and the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not
martingales. ∎

19.text:
The two baskets have the same 10 % p.a. drift in the mean and the same
stationary zero mean innovations once the deterministic trend is removed.
In price levels

$E\big[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}s> P^{B}_{t}$ ,
$E\big[P^{A}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{A}_{t}+0.10P_{0}s$ ,

so in levels both are 10 % sub-martingales, not martingales, and
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$ on a fixed calendar date.  A is the zero
variance limit of the law, $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s. in the
linear wording, $V^{A}_{*}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s., so $E$ and $H$ are false
pathwise and $B,C,D,F$ are false as price level martingale statements.

On $[30,31]$

$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.
and for $\sigma_{B}>0$

$E[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}] ,\qquad
E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$.

The running maximum is a strictly convex functional of the intra-year
shocks, $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$.  The 31st year is a free American /
look-back exercise window.  An ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted unwind can sell a
larger fraction of the remaining holding when $P^{B}_{t}$ is up in the
year and keep exposure when it is down.  With the stationary
mean-reverting part $X_{t}=P^{B}_{t}-a t$, $E[X_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]
=\rho_{s}X_{t}$ , $\rho_{s}<1$,

$E\big[P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=a(t+s)+ \rho_{s}X_{t}
<a(t+s)+X_{t}$  for $X_{t}>0$,

so a positive $X_{t}$ is expected to mean revert.  Putting more weight
on high $X_{t}$ realisations therefore raises

$E\Big[\int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{s}\Theta_{s}\,ds\Big]
=E\Big[\int_{30}^{31} a s\Theta_{s}\,ds\Big]+
E\Big[\int_{30}^{31}X_{s}\Theta_{s}\,ds\Big] $

above the drift-implied $E[P^{B}_{31}]$.  In textbook option-value
accounting

$E\big[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\big]=E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in[30,31]}
P^{B}_{\tau}\Big]=E[M_{31}]
 >E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]=P^{A}_{31}=E\big[V^{A}_{*}\big],$

the usual $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ convexity/timing premium created by the
$\pm20\%$ weekly volatility in the final year, which is identically zero
for the degenerate basket $A$, $\max_{[30,31]}P^{A}_{t}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.

The dominance is in expectation only: a realisation of $B$ can still lie
below the deterministic $A$ path, so pathwise $E$ and $H$ are false.
On a fixed terminal date the first moments coincide, $E[P^{B}_{T}]
=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, i.e. the $10\%$ p.a. average return is common to the two
baskets, and the price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales.
The strict in-expectation gain created by the 31st-year timing/look-back
option is

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}]$, the premium being purely ex-ante
and not pathwise.  This is the conventional $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$
volatility/timing effect; the mean-equivalence statement is the fixed
horizon content.

1.text:
Basket A is the zero variance limit of the 10 % p.a. drift law and Basket B
is the strictly positive variance realisation of the same law.  In
returns space

$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}1.10^{-t}$

is stationary zero mean

$E\big[\tilde P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=\tilde P_{t}$,
$E\big[P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P_{t},$

so in price levels both baskets are 10 % sub-martingales.  On a fixed
calendar date

$E\big[P_{T}^{B}\big]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E\big[P_{T}^{A}\big]$

and the price level itself is not a martingale, so the martingale
premises in B,C,D,F are false in levels.  A is a.s. deterministic so F
is false and a pathwise domination is impossible, so E and H are false.

On $[30,31]$ put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_{t}^{B}\ge P_{31}^{B}$ a.s.
With $\sigma_{B}>0$ weekly $M_{31}>P_{31}^{B}$ with positive probability
and

$E\big[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]>E\big[P_{31}^{B}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big],\qquad
E[M_{31}]>E[P_{31}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}.$

$E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ is the usual Jensen/convexity effect.  An
${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted unwind can be made path dependent and can sell a
larger fraction of the remaining holding when the intra-year price is up
and a smaller fraction when it is down.  The 31st year is therefore an
American/look-back exercise right on B which is identically zero for the
degenerate basket A, $\max_{[30,31]}P^{A}_{t}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.  In the
textbook option value accounting

$E\big[V^{B}_{\rm opt}\big]=E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in[30,31]}P^{B}_{\tau}\Big]
   =E[M_{31}]>E\big[P^{B}_{31}\big]
   =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*}=E\big[V^{A}_{*}\big],$

i.e. the volatile drifted basket commands a strictly positive
volatility/timing premium over the volatility free basket in expectation.
The premium is in expectation only: a realisation of $B$ can still lie
below the deterministic $A$ path so a necessary pathwise domination is
not obtained.  On a fixed terminal date the first moments coincide,
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, the usual mean preserving volatility
statement, with A the zero variance case of the common $10\%$ drift
mean.  The strict in-expectation gain created by the intra-year timing
right is the statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with the dominance being purely ex-ante and not pathwise, and with the
fixed horizon mean equivalence $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$ being the
content of the drift adjusted martingale remark.  On the literal
arithmetic-linear wording $P_{t}=P_{0}[1+0.10t]$ used in the statement
the first moment equivalence is $E[P^{B}_{T}]=P^{A}_{T}$ and the
geometric-vs-arithmetic $1.10^{T}>1+0.10T$ gap is the source of the
$A$ camp.

12.text:
Basket A is the zero-variance limit of the 10% drift law and Basket B is the
strictly positive variance realisation of the same law.  In levels

$E\big[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P^{B}_{t},\qquad 
E\big[P^{B}_{T}\big]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E\big[P^{A}_{T}\big]$

so on a fixed calendar date the first moment is pinned by the drift alone
and $P^{A},P^{B}$ are 10% sub-martingales in levels.  A is
$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s. so $V^{A}_{*}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s. and
$E$ and $H$ are false pathwise.  The martingale language in B,C,D,F is
to be understood in drift-adjusted returns, not in price levels, and
$A$ is deterministic so $F$ is false.

The 31st year is an exercise window ${\cal T}_{31}\subset[30,31]$.
Put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}$.  With $\sigma_{B}>0$ weekly
$M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability and

$E[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}],\qquad
E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}$,

i.e. $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$.  The running maximum is a strictly convex
functional of the intra-year shocks.  An ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted unwind
can be made path dependent and can sell a larger fraction of the
remaining holding when $P^{B}_{t}$ is up in the year and keep exposure
when it is down.  The 31st year liquidation right is therefore the
usual American/look-back option which is identically zero for the
degenerate basket $A$, $\max_{[30,31]}P^{A}_{t}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.

Hence in the textbook option-value accounting

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in{\cal T}_{31}}P^{B}_{\tau}\Big]
   =E[M_{31}]
   >E[P^{B}_{31}]
   =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}],$

with strict inequality as soon as $\operatorname{Var}(P^{B})>0$.  The
dominance is in expectation only: a realisation of $B$ can still lie
below the deterministic $A$ path so a necessary pathwise domination
and $E,H$ are false, and on a fixed terminal date the two baskets have
the common $10\%$ drift mean $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$.

That is the in-expectation timing/look-back premium of the volatile
drifted basket over the volatility-free basket,

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

the $31$-st year American option created by the $\pm20\%$ weekly
volatility.  The fixed-horizon first moment is the same $10\%$ drift for
the two baskets, which is the content of the mean-equivalence remark
commonly phrased as C.

8.text:
Basket A is the zero variance limit of the 10 % p.a. drift law and basket B is the
non-degenerate realisation of the same law.

In drift adjusted coordinates

$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}1.10^{-t}$ 

$E[\tilde P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=\tilde P_{t}$,

so that in levels

$E[P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=1.10^{s}P_{t}>P_{t}$

for both baskets.  In price levels $P^{A},P^{B}$ are $10\%$ sub-martingales,
not martingales, $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s. and $E[P^{B}_{T}]
=P_{0}1.10^{T}$ on any fixed calendar date.  On a fixed terminal date the
two baskets are therefore mean equivalent,

$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]=P_{0}1.10^{T},$

and $A$ is the degenerate zero-variance case of the common $10\%$ drift
mean.  Pathwise domination is impossible, $E$ and $H$ are false and the
price level martingale premises in $B,C,D,F$ are false in levels; $A$ is
a.s. deterministic so $F$ is false.

The 31st year is an American/look-back exercise window
${\cal T}_{31}=\{\tau:30\le\tau\le31\;{\cal F}$-adapted$\}$.
Put $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.  With
$\sigma_{B}>0$ weekly noise the running maximum is non-degenerate,

$M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive probability

and

$E[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}],\qquad
E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31},$

i.e. $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ the usual Jensen/convexity effect.  An
${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted unwind can be made a strictly convex functional
of the intra-year shocks, selling a larger fraction of the remaining
holding when $P^{B}_{t}$ is up in the year and keeping exposure when it
is down.  The in-year timing right is therefore the strictly positive
American/look-back option created by the $\pm20\%$ weekly volatility
which is identically zero for the degenerate basket $A$,
$\max_{[30,31]}P^{A}_{t}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.

In textbook option-value accounting

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]=E\Big[\sup_{\tau\in{\cal T}_{31}}P^{B}_{\tau}\Big]
      =E[M_{31}]
      >E[P^{B}_{31}]
      =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}],$

with strict inequality as soon as $\operatorname{Var}(P^{B})>0$.
The dominance is in expectation only: a realisation of $B$ can still
lie below the deterministic $A$ path, so a necessary pathwise
domination and $E,H$ are false, the price levels are $10\%$
sub-martingales so $B,C,D,F$ are false on their price-level martingale
premise, and on a fixed terminal date $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$.
The strictly positive intra-year timing/look-back premium of the
volatile drifted basket over the deterministic basket is the in-expectation
dominance

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with the familiar fixed-horizon mean equivalence
$E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}$.  On the literal
additive ARIMA-drift reading $P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+X_{t}$ the same
argument gives first-moment equality on a fixed date and the
conventional arithmetic-vs-geometric remark $1.10^{T}>1+0.10T$,
i.e. the $A$ strict mean-level dominance under the additive-mean
wording. ∎

6.text:
Basket A is the zero variance limit of the law that B is a draw from.
In levels, after removing the known deterministic drift,

$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}/1.10^{t}$ ,  $E[\tilde P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]
   =\tilde P_{t}$ ,

i.e. in returns space the innovations are stationary zero mean.
In levels

$E\big[P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P_{t}$ ,

so $P$ is a $10\%$ sub-martingale for both baskets.  A is the degenerate
realisation $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s., B is the high variance
realisation with the same drift.  On a fixed calendar date

$E\big[P^{B}_{T}\big]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E\big[P^{A}_{T}\big]$ .

Liquidation in year $31$ is an ${\cal F}_{t}$–adapted average

$V=\int_{0}^{1}P_{30+s}\Theta_{s}ds$, $\Theta_{s}\ge0,\;\int_{0}^{1}\Theta_{s}ds=1$,

or a bounded adapted stop $\tau\in[30,31]$.  By Fubini and the drift
property

$E\big[V\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]=P_{30}\,
E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\mid{\cal F}_{30}\right]$

and unconditionally

$E[V]=E[P_{30}]\,E\!\left[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\right]
     =P_{0}1.10^{31}$

and for a stop $E[P_{\tau}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]=1.10^{\tau-30}P_{30}$.
Optional stopping for the drift adjusted martingale preserves the mean
on the bounded interval $[30,31]$.  The best you can do in expectation is
to put weight at the latest feasible time, i.e. the drift implied mean
$P_{0}1.10^{31}$.  The $\pm20\%$ weekly moves are zero mean stationary
noise around the trend.  They change dispersion, skewness and the shape
of the outcome but they do not move the unconditional first moment.

It is true pathwise that

$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}\ {\rm a.s.}$,
$E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$,

i.e. $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$.  $M_{31}$ is not ${\cal F}_{t}$-measurable;
the supremum cannot be locked in without foresight.  Any admissible
non-anticipative unwind averages the zero mean noise and the average of
stationary zero mean noise is zero in expectation.  Volatility therefore
raises dispersion and the realised look-back benefit on some paths, it
does not create a systematic unconditional mean premium.

Hence in the conventional $E[\cdot]$ sense the deterministic basket A is
the zero variance realisation of the common $10\%$ drift mean that B
attains in expectation.  The two strategies are mean equivalent with the
common expected liquidation wealth $P_{0}1.10^{31}$.  In the language of
the list that is the stationary returns / drift adjusted martingale
content, the same average return and the same unconditional expected
value for the two baskets, i.e. C, B being the weaker average-return
form.  Price levels are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales, so the
martingale wording is properly understood as drift adjusted returns;
pathwise necessary domination $E,H$ and the strict in-expectation
dominance $G$ and the strict $A$ dominance are false in the
arithmetic-linear reading used in the statement. ∎

15.text:
The 10 % p.a. number is the first moment of the two laws.  After the
known deterministic trend is removed

$\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}/1.10^{t}$ ,  $E[\tilde P_{t+s}\mid {\cal F}_{t}]=\tilde
P_{t}$ , 

is the zero-mean stationary return law that the statement refers to.
In price levels

$E\big[P_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=1.10^{s}P_{t}$

for A and for B, so that in levels both baskets are 10 % sub-martingales.
A is the degenerate zero-variance realisation of the common law,

$P_{t}^{A}=P_{0}1.10^{t}\ {\rm a.s.}$ ,

and B is the high-variance realisation of the same law.  On any fixed
calendar date

$E[P_{T}^{B}]=P_{0}1.10^{T}=E[P_{T}^{A}]$

and in the linear-trend wording used in the statement
$E[P_{T}^{B}]=P_{0}[1+0.10T]=P_{T}^{A}$.  The $ \pm 20\%$ weekly moves
are zero mean stationary noise around the 10 % trend.

Let $\Theta_{s}\ge0$, $\int_{0}^{1}\Theta_{s}ds=1$, be an ${\cal
F}_{30+s}$-adapted liquidation intensity on the 31st year and
$V=\int_{0}^{1}P_{30+s}\Theta_{s}ds$.  By Fubini

$E\big[V\mid{\cal F}_{30}\big]=P_{30}\,
E\Big[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\mid{\cal F}_{30}\Big]$

and unconditionally

$E[V]=E[P_{30}]\,E\Big[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\Big]
      =P_{0}1.10^{30}E\Big[\int_{0}^{1}1.10^{s}\Theta_{s}ds\Big]$ .

The only thing that can move the first moment is the deterministic
factor $1.10^{s}$.  Optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale
$\tilde P_{t}$ gives for any adapted $\tau\in[30,31]$

$E[P_{\tau}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]=1.10^{\tau-30}P_{30}$,

so that on the bounded interval $[30,31]$ the conditional mean is
maximised by $\tau\equiv31$.  The best you can do in expectation with an
adapted average or stopped liquidation is therefore the drift implied
mean

$E[V^{A}_{*}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=E[P^{B}_{31}]$,

and any admissible adapted unwind has $E[V^{B}]\le E[P^{B}_{31}]$.  In
particular the $E[\sup_{[30,31]}P^{B}]>\sup_{[30,31]}E[P^{B}]$ convexity
is a genuine pathwise distributional effect,

$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.,  $E[M_{31}]
>E[P^{B}_{31}]$,

but $M_{31}$ is not ${\cal F}_{t}$-attainable.  The supremum is an
ex-post look-back redistribution of probability mass; it cannot be
locked in by a non-anticipative liquidation that has to unwind over the
whole 31st year.  Averaging a zero-mean stationary noise does not move
the first moment.

Hence volatility changes dispersion, skewness and the shape of the
outcome, not the unconditional first moment.  Basket A is the zero-
variance realisation of the common 10 % drift mean that Basket B has in
expectation.  In the conventional $E[\cdot]$ sense the two strategies are
mean equivalent with the common 10 % p.a. average return and the same
unconditional expected liquidation wealth $P_{0}1.10^{31}$, i.e. the
drift-adjusted martingale / stationary-return statement.  The price
levels themselves are 10 % sub-martingales, so the literal price-level
martingale wording is false, pathwise domination $E,H$ is impossible and
the in-expectation volatility premium $G$ is not attainable by an
${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted liquidation.  This is the content of the
stationary-return mean preservation, $B$ in the return sense and $C$ for
the expected liquidation value. ∎

3.text:
Basket A is the zero-variance limit of the 10 % p.a. drift law and Basket B is the
strictly positive variance realisation of the same law.

In levels with the linear trend that the statement writes down

* $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t$ a.s.  $V^{A}_{*}=P^{A}_{31}$ a.s.
* $P^{B}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t+X_{t}$ , $E[X_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=X_{t}$,
  $E\big[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}\big]=P^{B}_{t}+0.10P_{0}s$ .

Hence after de-trending $\tilde P_{t}=P_{t}-0.10P_{0}t$ is stationary zero-mean
and $P^{A},P^{B}$ are $10\%$ sub-martingales in levels.  On a fixed calendar
date

$E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}T=P^{A}_{T}$,

so the $10\%$ p.a. drift is common to the two baskets and on a fixed
terminal date the first moments coincide.  A is deterministic so F is false
and a pathwise domination is impossible, so E and H are false.  The
price-level martingale premises in B,C,D are false in levels; the
martingale property holds for the drift-adjusted returns.

The 31st year is an American / look-back exercise window
${\cal T}_{31}=\{\tau:30\le \tau\le31\;{\cal F}\hbox{-adapted}\}$.
Put

$M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}\ {\rm a.s.}$

With $\sigma_{B}>0$ weekly $\pm20\%$ moves $M_{31}>P^{B}_{31}$ with positive
probability and

$E[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}],\qquad
E[M_{31}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}31$ ,

$E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$ the usual strict convexity / Jensen effect.
The running maximum is a strictly convex functional of the intra-year
shocks.  An ${\cal F}_{t}$-adapted unwind can be made path dependent and
can sell a larger fraction of the remaining holding when $P^{B}_{t}$ is up
in the year and keep exposure when it is down.  In the textbook
option-value accounting the 31st-year liquidation right is the
American/look-back option

$V^{B}_{\rm opt}= \sup_{\tau\in [30,31]}P^{B}_{\tau}$,

with

$E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]
 =E\Big[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\Big]
 =E[M_{31}]
 >E[P^{B}_{31}]
 =P_{0}+0.10P_{0}31
 =V^{A}_{*}=E[V^{A}_{*}]$

the strict inequality holding as soon as $\operatorname{Var}(P^{B})>0$.
The premium is in expectation only: a realisation of $B$ can still lie
below the deterministic $A$ path, so a necessary pathwise domination is
absent and E,H are false.  On a fixed terminal date the two baskets have
the common $10\%$ drift mean $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$, the price levels
are $10\%$ sub-martingales, not martingales, so B,C,D,F are false on their
price-level martingale premise and A is deterministic so F is false.

That is the in-expectation dominance of the volatile drifted basket over
the degenerate basket created by the 31st-year timing / look-back option,
i.e.

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with $E[V^{B}_{\rm opt}]>E[V^{A}_{*}]$.  On the fixed-horizon first
moment the two baskets are mean equivalent, $E[P^{B}_{T}]=E[P^{A}_{T}]$,
which is the content usually quoted as C. ∎

18.text:
Basket A is the zero-variance limit of the 10 % p.a. drift law and Basket B
is the same 10 % p.a. drift law with strictly positive stationary zero-mean
innovations.  In levels

I think the drift-adjusted martingale point that colleagues 13,14,15,16,17,2,21,5,7,9 are making is the right way to read the set-up and it resolves the apparent convexity intuition.

Both baskets are specified to have a known 10% p.a. linear growth trend and stationary, zero-mean return innovations with constant long-run autocovariance. After de-trending

$\tilde P_t = P_t /1.10^{\,t}$,

we have $E[\tilde P_{t+s}\mid\mathcal F_t]=\tilde P_t$, i.e. returns are stationary and drift-adjusted martingale. In levels $E[P_{t+s}\mid\mathcal F_t]=1.10^{\,s}P_t$ for A and for B. A is the degenerate zero-variance realisation of that law, B is the high-variance realisation. Price levels are 10% sub-martingales for both, so the level-martingale wording is properly understood in returns space.

Liquidation in the 31st year is an $\mathcal F_t$-adapted unwind, not a free ex-post choice of the pathwise peak. Write a feasible plan as $V=\int_{0}^{1}P_{30+s}\Theta_s ds$ with $\Theta_s\ge0$, $\int_0^1\Theta_s ds=1$, $\Theta$ adapted. By Fubini and the drift property

$E[V\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=P_{30}\,E\big[\int_0^1 1.10^{\,s}\Theta_s ds\mid\mathcal F_{30}\big]$,

so unconditionally $E[V]=E[P_{30}]E[\int_0^11.10^{\,s}\Theta_s ds]$. The $\pm20\%$ weekly moves are zero-mean stationary noise around the trend. They change dispersion, skewness and the shape of the outcome; they do not change the conditional mean $E[P_{30+s}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=1.10^{\,s}P_{30}$.

It is true that pathwise $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_t^B\ge P_{31}^B$ a.s. and $E[M_{31}]>E[P_{31}^B]$. That is $E[\sup P]>\sup E[P]$, a genuine distributional convexity statement about the running maximum. The supremum is not $\mathcal F_t$-measurable and cannot be locked in by an adapted liquidation that has to unwind over the course of the year. Any admissible adapted average or stopping $\tau\in[30,31]$ satisfies $E[P_\tau\mid\mathcal F_{30}]=1.10^{\tau-30}P_{30}$, and optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale preserves the first moment on a bounded interval.
